entries.meaning: To stop sleeping, or to rouse someone from sleep — a more literary word than wake up — and, figuratively, to stir something that was dormant.
examples: I awake before the alarm most mornings.
She awoke to the sound of rain on the roof.
The whole house had awoken by six.
Try not to awake the children when you come in.
The sirens awoke half the neighborhood.
The dog has awoken me at dawn every day this week.
Something in the story awoke an old memory.
Small kindnesses awake loyalty in people.
The photographs have awoken a homesickness she thought was gone.
The country slowly awoke to the scale of the problem.
We awake to our mistakes only after the fact.
Investors have awoken to the risk.

senses.head: Stop sleeping
body: Intransitive and a little literary; everyday American speech says wake up. Keep it apart from the adjective awake — I was awake at four is a state, not a past tense. (просыпаться, пробуждаться)
examples: I awake before the alarm most mornings.
She awoke to the sound of rain on the roof.
The whole house had awoken by six.

senses.head: Wake someone up
body: Transitive, and rarer than the intransitive sense; most American writers reach for wake or the regular awaken here. (будить, разбудить)
examples: Try not to awake the children when you come in.
The sirens awoke half the neighborhood.
The dog has awoken me at dawn every day this week.

senses.head: Stir up a feeling or memory
body: Figurative and transitive, common in writing: a sight, a smell, or a story brings something dormant back to life. (пробуждать (чувства, воспоминания))
examples: Something in the story awoke an old memory.
Small kindnesses awake loyalty in people.
The photographs have awoken a homesickness she thought was gone.

senses.head: awake to — become aware of
body: Followed by a noun: to finally see something you had been ignoring. The adjective version, be awake to, is at least as common. (осознать, понять)
examples: The country slowly awoke to the scale of the problem.
We awake to our mistakes only after the fact.
Investors have awoken to the risk.

entries.register: neutral to formal — ordinary in writing; everyday speech says wake up
entries.third person: awakes · -ing form: awaking (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: Awake follows wake exactly, and carries the same traps. It is also an adjective — I was awake at four is a state, not a past tense — and it has a regular cousin awaken/awakened/awakened, which is what most American writers reach for. The past cannot serve as the participle: ✗ had awoke, ✓ had awoken.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and literary beside everyday wake up; keep the verb apart from the adjective awake (I was awake at four is a state, not a past tense)
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive when you stop sleeping (she awoke to the sound of rain), transitive when you rouse someone or stir a feeling (the sirens awoke half the neighborhood); awake to takes a prepositional object
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — half the neighborhood was awoken by the sirens, an old homesickness has been awoken. No passive of the intransitive she awoke.

entries.meaning: To carry or support something, to endure it, or to bring it forth — plus the passive be born, the one sense that takes born instead of borne.
examples: I can't bear the sound of a dentist's drill.
She bore the delay without a word of complaint.
He has borne worse news than this.
Their twins were born in a snowstorm.
He was born the year the mill closed.
All three of her children had been born by the time she turned thirty.
Mares usually bear one foal at a time.
She bore three children in five years.
The queen had borne no heir.
These beams bear the weight of the whole roof.
The ice bore his weight for two steps and then cracked.
The company has borne the legal fees since March.
The servers bear trays over their heads.
The messengers bore the news from the capital.
Pilgrims have borne these relics along the same road for centuries.
The old apple tree bears less fruit every year.
The account bore four percent interest.
Two years of talks have borne fruit at last.
The building bears her grandfather's name.
The check bore no signature.
The town has borne that name since 1802.
Bear in mind that the office closes at four.
We bore in mind that she was new.
The committee has borne the deadline in mind throughout.
Bear with me — this will take a minute.
She bore with his questions for a full hour.
Readers have borne with this digression long enough.
Bear left where the road forks.
The trail bore east along the ridge.
We had borne too far south and lost the river.
The data bear out her theory.
The audit bore out every complaint.
Events have borne him out.

senses.head: Endure, put up with
body: Very often negative or with can't: I can't bear it. The participle is borne, never born. (терпеть, выносить)
examples: I can't bear the sound of a dentist's drill.
She bore the delay without a word of complaint.
He has borne worse news than this.

senses.head: be born (passive only)
body: Passive only, and the only sense spelled born. There is no active ✗ she borned; birth in the active takes bear/bore/borne. (родиться)
examples: Their twins were born in a snowstorm.
He was born the year the mill closed.
All three of her children had been born by the time she turned thirty.

senses.head: Give birth to, bring forth
body: The active birth sense, formal or literary; ordinary speech says have a baby. Here the participle is borne: She has borne three children. (рожать, родить)
examples: Mares usually bear one foal at a time.
She bore three children in five years.
The queen had borne no heir.

senses.head: Carry the weight of, support
body: The structural sense — of beams, walls, ice, or a person carrying a burden or a cost. (нести (нагрузку), выдерживать вес)
examples: These beams bear the weight of the whole roof.
The ice bore his weight for two steps and then cracked.
The company has borne the legal fees since March.

senses.head: Carry, bring (formal)
body: Formal or literary for physically carrying something from one place to another — bearing gifts, bearing a message. (нести, приносить)
examples: The servers bear trays over their heads.
The messengers bore the news from the capital.
Pilgrims have borne these relics along the same road for centuries.

senses.head: Produce, yield
body: Of trees, investments, and efforts. Bear fruit works literally and figuratively; bear interest is the banking use. (приносить (плоды, доход, результат))
examples: The old apple tree bears less fruit every year.
The account bore four percent interest.
Two years of talks have borne fruit at last.

senses.head: Have or show (a name, mark, resemblance)
body: Of documents, buildings, and faces: to carry a name, a signature, a scar, or a likeness. (носить (имя, знак), иметь)
examples: The building bears her grandfather's name.
The check bore no signature.
The town has borne that name since 1802.

senses.head: bear in mind
body: A fixed phrase, most often imperative, meaning to keep a fact in view while deciding something. (иметь в виду, учитывать)
examples: Bear in mind that the office closes at four.
We bore in mind that she was new.
The committee has borne the deadline in mind throughout.

senses.head: bear with (someone)
body: A request for patience, usually imperative: bear with me. (потерпеть, отнестись с терпением)
examples: Bear with me — this will take a minute.
She bore with his questions for a full hour.
Readers have borne with this digression long enough.

senses.head: Turn, veer in a direction
body: Of a road, a vehicle, or a walker; also nautical. Bear left, bear right, bear north. (брать (влево, вправо), держать курс)
examples: Bear left where the road forks.
The trail bore east along the ridge.
We had borne too far south and lost the river.

senses.head: bear out — confirm
body: Of evidence, data, or events proving a claim or a person right. (подтверждать)
examples: The data bear out her theory.
The audit bore out every complaint.
Events have borne him out.

entries.register: everyday — can't bear it and was born are in every American's mouth
entries.contrast: English keeps two participles here and they are not interchangeable. Born belongs to birth, and only in the passive: She was born in Ohio. Every other sense — carrying, enduring, producing — takes borne: He has borne the cost alone, The plan has borne fruit. The base is also a homophone of the adjective bare.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the carrying, enduring, and producing senses; closer to stative in bear a name / bear a resemblance / bear interest, where the progressive is odd: ✗ the building is bearing her name
entries.transitivity: both — transitive almost everywhere (bear the cost, bear three children, bear fruit), intransitive in the direction sense (bear left where the road forks)
entries.passive: restricted — natural for costs and burdens (the legal fees have been borne by the company), and be born is passive-only (she was born in Ohio; there is no active ✗ she borned). But the name and resemblance senses resist it: ✗ her grandfather's name is borne by the building, and ✗ left was borne at the fork.
entries.phrasal verbs: bear down · bear down on · bear on · bear out · bear up · bear with

entries.meaning: A formal, literary verb meaning to be evidence of something; its past form bespoke leads a second life as a British adjective for custom-made goods.
examples: Cracked paint and a sagging porch bespeak neglect.
The empty shelves bespoke a store about to close.
The silence had bespoken trouble long before anyone admitted it.
Her steady voice bespeaks years of practice.
He bespoke a suit from a tailor on Savile Row.
In older novels a traveler would bespeak dinner at the inn.
The rooms had been bespoken months before the wedding.
He wears a bespoke suit to every hearing.
The firm sells bespoke software to hospitals.

senses.head: Be a sign of, give evidence of
body: The only living verb sense in American English, and formal even then. The subject is almost always a thing — a voice, a room, a detail — not a person. (свидетельствовать о, говорить о)
examples: Cracked paint and a sagging porch bespeak neglect.
The empty shelves bespoke a store about to close.
The silence had bespoken trouble long before anyone admitted it.
Her steady voice bespeaks years of practice.

senses.head: Order or arrange in advance
body: Archaic: to speak for something ahead of time — a suit, a room, a dinner. This is the sense that produced the tailoring adjective. (заказывать заранее, договариваться о)
examples: He bespoke a suit from a tailor on Savile Row.
In older novels a traveler would bespeak dinner at the inn.
The rooms had been bespoken months before the wedding.

senses.head: bespoke — custom-made (adjective)
body: British, and not a verb use at all, though it is where most readers meet the form. Americans say custom-made, made-to-order, or custom. (сделанный на заказ, индивидуальный)
examples: He wears a bespoke suit to every hearing.
The firm sells bespoke software to hospitals.

entries.register: rare — a prefixed, literary verb; bespoke is better known as the British tailoring adjective
entries.contrast: A prefixed speak — the same three forms with be- on the front, so there is nothing new to memorize. In American English it is a formal, literary verb meaning "be evidence of," and the past form bespoke is far better known as a British adjective for custom tailoring (a bespoke suit); Americans say custom-made.
entries.verb type: stative in its one living American sense, "be evidence of" — the subject is a thing, not an actor, and the progressive is out: ✗ the silence is bespeaking trouble. The archaic "order in advance" sense is action
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory: cracked paint bespeaks neglect, ✗ the empty shelves bespoke
entries.passive: restricted — fine in the archaic ordering sense (the rooms had been bespoken months before the wedding), but the evidence sense resists it like other stative verbs: ✗ neglect is bespoken by the cracked paint.

entries.meaning: To cut or grip something with the teeth — and, by extension, to sting, to grip a surface, or to take hold painfully.
examples: Dogs bite when they are frightened.
The neighbor's terrier bit the mail carrier last spring.
I have bitten my nails since I was nine.
Mosquitoes bite worst at dusk.
The mosquito bit me twice before I felt it.
She was bitten by a spider in the garage.
Winter tires bite into packed snow.
The blade bit deep into the log.
The anchor had bitten into the sand by then.
The wind bites on that side of the building.
By then the cold had bitten through my gloves.
The new tariffs bit hardest in the smallest towns.
Trout bite best just after sunrise.
We advertised for a week and nobody bit.
Two buyers have bitten since we dropped the price.
You'll have to bite the bullet and tell her.
We finally bit the bullet and replaced the roof.
He has bitten the bullet on far worse repairs.
I bit my tongue and said nothing.
She had to bite back a laugh.
He has bitten his tongue through three straight meetings.

senses.head: Cut or grip with the teeth
body: The core sense, transitive or intransitive. Remember the split: past bit, participle bitten — ✗ I have bit my tongue. (кусать, укусить)
examples: Dogs bite when they are frightened.
The neighbor's terrier bit the mail carrier last spring.
I have bitten my nails since I was nine.

senses.head: Sting (of insects and snakes)
body: In American usage mosquitoes, spiders, ants, and snakes bite; bees and wasps sting. (кусать, жалить)
examples: Mosquitoes bite worst at dusk.
The mosquito bit me twice before I felt it.
She was bitten by a spider in the garage.

senses.head: Grip a surface, take hold
body: Of tires, blades, screws, and anchors — anything that digs in rather than slipping. (врезаться, впиваться, цепляться)
examples: Winter tires bite into packed snow.
The blade bit deep into the log.
The anchor had bitten into the sand by then.

senses.head: Take effect painfully
body: Of cold, wind, budget cuts, sanctions, or prices — the moment something stops being abstract and starts to hurt. (сказываться, бить (по кому-л.), пробирать)
examples: The wind bites on that side of the building.
By then the cold had bitten through my gloves.
The new tariffs bit hardest in the smallest towns.

senses.head: Take the bait, respond to an offer
body: Of fish, and figuratively of buyers or of anyone falling for a trick. Often negative: nobody bit. (клюнуть, попасться на удочку)
examples: Trout bite best just after sunrise.
We advertised for a week and nobody bit.
Two buyers have bitten since we dropped the price.

senses.head: bite the bullet
body: A fixed phrase: to accept something painful you have been putting off. (стиснуть зубы, решиться на неприятное)
examples: You'll have to bite the bullet and tell her.
We finally bit the bullet and replaced the roof.
He has bitten the bullet on far worse repairs.

senses.head: bite your tongue, bite back
body: To stop yourself from saying something. Bite back takes an object: bite back a reply. (прикусить язык, сдержаться)
examples: I bit my tongue and said nothing.
She had to bite back a laugh.
He has bitten his tongue through three straight meetings.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.third person: bites · -ing form: biting (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: The past is bit and the participle is bitten: ✗ I have bit my tongue, ✓ I have bitten my tongue. Because bit is also an everyday noun (a bit of sugar) and a past tense that sounds complete on its own, the short form slips in after have more than almost any other verb in this group.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, from teeth (the terrier bit the mail carrier) to tires gripping snow to cold and tariffs taking hold
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with an object (bite your tongue, bite back a laugh), intransitive with the object left out (dogs bite, nobody bit, the wind bites)
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — she was bitten by a spider in the garage. No passive of the intransitive trout bite best after sunrise.
entries.phrasal verbs: bite back · bite into · bite off

entries.meaning: To separate something into pieces or stop it working — and, figuratively, to violate a rule, interrupt a state, or surpass a limit.
examples: Glass jars break if you stack them.
He broke the vase reaching for the light.
Someone had broken the window before we arrived.
Cheap chargers break within a month.
My phone broke the day the warranty ended.
The washing machine has broken twice this year.
Old bones break easily.
He broke his wrist on the ice last winter.
She has broken the same finger twice.
Don't break your promise to her.
The company broke the terms of the lease.
He has broken every rule in the handbook.
Nobody wanted to break the silence.
A branch broke his fall.
The rain has broken the heat wave at last.
Records break at every Olympics.
She broke the state record in the 400.
Three runners have broken four minutes on this track.
She breaks the news gently whenever she can.
The paper broke the story on Sunday.
Someone had broken the news to him already.
Day breaks around five in June.
His voice broke when he thanked her.
The storm had broken before we reached the car.
Break the costs down by department.
Our car broke down on the interstate.
The talks have broken down completely.
Ice on the river breaks up in April.
They broke up after four years.
The meeting had broken up by noon.
It takes a week to break in new boots.
Someone broke into the garage last night.
Thieves have broken into three cars on this block.
Fires break out in that canyon every August.
War broke out that September.
Two inmates had broken out through the laundry.

senses.head: Break into pieces, smash
body: The literal core, transitive or intransitive. After have it is always broken: ✗ I have broke it. (ломать, разбивать; ломаться)
examples: Glass jars break if you stack them.
He broke the vase reaching for the light.
Someone had broken the window before we arrived.

senses.head: Stop working, fail
body: Of machines and devices. For cars and larger machinery Americans usually add down. (ломаться, выходить из строя)
examples: Cheap chargers break within a month.
My phone broke the day the warranty ended.
The washing machine has broken twice this year.

senses.head: Fracture a bone
body: Used of the person and of the bone alike: he broke his wrist, his wrist broke. (сломать (кость))
examples: Old bones break easily.
He broke his wrist on the ice last winter.
She has broken the same finger twice.

senses.head: Violate a rule, law, or promise
body: Figurative but completely ordinary — break the law, break a contract, break your word. (нарушать (закон, обещание, правило))
examples: Don't break your promise to her.
The company broke the terms of the lease.
He has broken every rule in the handbook.

senses.head: Interrupt, put an end to a continuous state
body: Of silence, a habit, a tie, a heat wave, a fall, a journey — anything that has been running unbroken. (прерывать, нарушать (тишину, привычку, ничью))
examples: Nobody wanted to break the silence.
A branch broke his fall.
The rain has broken the heat wave at last.

senses.head: Beat a record or a limit
body: Of records, thresholds, and numbers: break a record, break four minutes, break a hundred degrees. (побить (рекорд), преодолеть (порог))
examples: Records break at every Olympics.
She broke the state record in the 400.
Three runners have broken four minutes on this track.

senses.head: break the news, break a story
body: To be the one who tells something for the first time — gently, in the case of bad news; first, in the case of journalism. (сообщить (новость), первым опубликовать)
examples: She breaks the news gently whenever she can.
The paper broke the story on Sunday.
Someone had broken the news to him already.

senses.head: Of dawn, weather, or a voice
body: A cluster of intransitive uses: day breaks, a storm breaks, and a voice breaks either with emotion or in adolescence. (наступать (о рассвете); разразиться; ломаться (о голосе))
examples: Day breaks around five in June.
His voice broke when he thanked her.
The storm had broken before we reached the car.

senses.head: break down
body: Three common uses: a vehicle or negotiation fails, a person loses composure, or something is separated into parts for analysis. (сломаться; сорваться, разрыдаться; разбить на части)
examples: Break the costs down by department.
Our car broke down on the interstate.
The talks have broken down completely.

senses.head: break up
body: To end a relationship, to disperse a gathering, or to come apart into pieces. Of a phone call it means the signal is cutting out. (расстаться; разойтись; распадаться)
examples: Ice on the river breaks up in April.
They broke up after four years.
The meeting had broken up by noon.

senses.head: break in, break into
body: Break into a building or a car is burglary; break in also means to soften new shoes or train a newcomer, and break into a market or a laugh starts something abruptly. (вломиться, проникнуть; разносить (обувь))
examples: It takes a week to break in new boots.
Someone broke into the garage last night.
Thieves have broken into three cars on this block.

senses.head: break out
body: Of fires, wars, arguments, and epidemics starting suddenly; also of escaping from confinement, and of skin — break out in a rash. (вспыхнуть (о войне, пожаре); сбежать)
examples: Fires break out in that canyon every August.
War broke out that September.
Two inmates had broken out through the laundry.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: ✗ I have broke it — after have, it is always broken. Bare broke doubles as an adjective meaning "out of money" (I'm broke until Friday), which is part of why the wrong form sounds passable to some ears. The base is a homophone of brake.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and ergative: the same event runs transitive or intransitive (he broke the vase / the vase broke). Bare broke also lives on as an adjective, "out of money"
entries.transitivity: both — transitive when someone breaks a thing, a rule, or a record (she broke the state record), intransitive of things that break, fail, or begin (my phone broke, day breaks around five, war broke out)
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the window had been broken before we arrived, the story was broken on Sunday. No passive of the intransitive day breaks or the talks broke down.
entries.phrasal verbs: break away · break down · break even · break in · break into · break off · break out · break out of · break through · break up · break with

entries.meaning: To pick one thing out of several, or to decide on a course of action.
examples: You choose the restaurant this time.
They chose the cheaper apartment.
We have chosen a name for the dog.
People choose to live here for the quiet.
She chose to walk rather than wait for the bus.
He has chosen not to comment.
Each team chooses a captain in September.
Voters chose him by a wide margin.
The committee had chosen her before the interviews ended.
You have to choose between the two offers.
She chose from a list of six.
I have chosen from this menu so often I know it by heart.
He acts like the chosen one.
They saw themselves as a chosen people.

senses.head: Pick one out of several
body: The core sense. Watch the spelling more than the tense: present choose /tʃuz/, past chose /tʃoʊz/, and there is no ✗ choosed. (выбирать, выбрать)
examples: You choose the restaurant this time.
They chose the cheaper apartment.
We have chosen a name for the dog.

senses.head: choose to — decide to do something
body: With an infinitive, meaning to do something deliberately rather than by default. Often used to underline that it was a free decision. (предпочесть, решить)
examples: People choose to live here for the quiet.
She chose to walk rather than wait for the bus.
He has chosen not to comment.

senses.head: Select someone for a role
body: Of committees, voters, and teams. Very often passive: she was chosen from a field of forty. (избирать, отбирать, назначать)
examples: Each team chooses a captain in September.
Voters chose him by a wide margin.
The committee had chosen her before the interviews ended.

senses.head: choose between, choose from
body: Between takes two options, among or from takes more. There is nothing to choose between them means they are equally good. (выбирать между; выбирать из)
examples: You have to choose between the two offers.
She chose from a list of six.
I have chosen from this menu so often I know it by heart.

senses.head: chosen — selected, elect (adjective)
body: As an adjective the participle carries a religious or elevated tone: the chosen people, the chosen one. (избранный)
examples: He acts like the chosen one.
They saw themselves as a chosen people.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.third person: chooses · -ing form: choosing (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: Two o's in the present, one in the past — and completely different vowels: choose /tʃuz/ but chose /tʃoʊz/. Since the spellings differ by a single letter, the common error is a misspelling rather than a tense mistake: ✗ I chose to walk to work every day when you mean choose. There is no ✗ choosed.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic mental verb; the progressive is fine (I'm still choosing). The participle chosen also stands alone as an elevated adjective: the chosen one
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the thing picked (they chose the cheaper apartment), intransitive when the object is understood (you choose this time) or replaced by between / from or a to-infinitive (she chose to walk)
entries.passive: yes — she was chosen from a field of forty, a captain is chosen every September. The to-infinitive pattern has no passive: ✗ to walk was chosen by her.

entries.meaning: Two unrelated verbs share this spelling with nearly opposite meanings — to split something apart, and to cling to it. Both are regular in modern American English; clove and cloven survive only in fixed phrases and older writing.
examples: Frost can cleave a boulder in half.
One blow clove the log in two.
Lightning had cloven the old oak from crown to root.
Today a writer would simply say the axe cleaved the log.
The jet cleaves the air with almost no noise.
The bow of the boat clove the water cleanly.
The prow had cloven a channel through the slush.
Goats and sheep have cloven hooves.
The devil is always drawn with a cloven foot.
She cleaves to the plan no matter what anyone says.
He cleaved to the old customs all his life.
They have cleaved to one another through worse than this.

senses.head: Split apart, chop in two
body: The living form is cleaved; clove and cloven are archaic and will read as deliberate old-fashioned style. (раскалывать, разрубать)
examples: Frost can cleave a boulder in half.
One blow clove the log in two.
Lightning had cloven the old oak from crown to root.
Today a writer would simply say the axe cleaved the log.

senses.head: Cut through water or air
body: Literary, of ships, blades, and aircraft moving cleanly through something. (рассекать)
examples: The jet cleaves the air with almost no noise.
The bow of the boat clove the water cleanly.
The prow had cloven a channel through the slush.

senses.head: cloven — split in two (adjective)
body: Survives almost entirely in cloven hoof and cloven foot, and so carries a faint biblical or devilish echo. (раздвоенный, расщепленный)
examples: Goats and sheep have cloven hooves.
The devil is always drawn with a cloven foot.

senses.head: cleave to — cling, stay faithful to
body: A separate verb that happens to be spelled the same; always regular (cleaved to), and formal or biblical in tone. (держаться (за), хранить верность)
examples: She cleaves to the plan no matter what anyone says.
He cleaved to the old customs all his life.
They have cleaved to one another through worse than this.

entries.register: rare — narrow and mostly frozen (cloven hoof, cleft palate); the living verb is regular cleaved
entries.third person: cleaves · -ing form: cleaving (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: Two unrelated verbs share this spelling with nearly opposite meanings — cleave "split apart" and cleave "cling to" — and in ordinary American English both are regular: cleaved, cleaved. The strong forms clove/cloven survive mainly in the fixed phrase cloven hoof, and the third variant cleft survives in cleft palate and a cleft in the rock. Learn the pattern here, but write cleaved.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both of the unrelated verbs that share this spelling, splitting and clinging; note that modern American English inflects both regularly (cleaved), with clove/cloven frozen in cloven hoof
entries.transitivity: both — transitive when you split something (one blow clove the log in two, the jet cleaves the air), intransitive with a preposition in cleave to (he cleaved to the old customs)
entries.passive: restricted — the splitting sense passivizes (the old oak had been cloven from crown to root), but cleave to is prepositional and resists it: ✗ the plan is cleaved to by her.

entries.meaning: To dig — today almost always figuratively, into records, a subject, or the bottom of a bag. The strong forms dolve and dolven are archaic; modern usage is regular.
examples: Historians delve into letters and diaries for the real story.
She delved into the archive for three months.
Reporters have delved into his tax records.
In older English the gardener dolve a trench along the wall.
Monks had dolven the well long before the abbey went up.
Miners have delved under these hills since the 1870s.
She delves in her bag for a pen at every register.
He delved in his coat for the tickets.
I have delved through this drawer twice already.

senses.head: delve into — research deeply
body: By far the commonest use, and fully regular: delve, delved, delved. Almost always with into. (углубляться в, копаться в (материале))
examples: Historians delve into letters and diaries for the real story.
She delved into the archive for three months.
Reporters have delved into his tax records.

senses.head: Dig in the ground
body: The original literal sense, now archaic, and the one that carries the old forms dolve and dolven you will meet in older poetry and Bible translations. (рыть, копать)
examples: In older English the gardener dolve a trench along the wall.
Monks had dolven the well long before the abbey went up.
Miners have delved under these hills since the 1870s.

senses.head: Reach in and rummage
body: Physical but small-scale: hunting through a bag, a drawer, or a pocket. Regular. (рыться (в сумке, кармане), шарить)
examples: She delves in her bag for a pen at every register.
He delved in his coat for the tickets.
I have delved through this drawer twice already.

entries.register: archaic — dolve and dolven are out of use; the living verb is regular delved
entries.third person: delves · -ing form: delving (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: Dolve and dolven are archaic. No American speaker uses them today; the living verb is fully regular — delve, delved, delved — and that is what you should write and say. The old forms are listed because they show this group's pattern perfectly, and because you will meet them in older poetry and in older Bible translations.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a digging verb that today survives almost entirely in the figurative delve into, with the strong forms dolve/dolven archaic
entries.transitivity: intransitive in all living American uses — the complement is a prepositional phrase, not an object: she delved into the archive, he delved in his coat for the tickets. Only the archaic literal sense took a direct object (the gardener dolve a trench)
entries.passive: no in modern usage — an intransitive verb has nothing to promote, and the prepositional passive is marginal at best: ✗ his tax records have been delved into. Only the archaic transitive digging sense allows one: the well had been dolven long before the abbey.

entries.meaning: To hold yourself back from doing something you could do — a formal verb, and the prefixed sibling of bear.
examples: Please forbear from calling before nine.
He forbore to mention the argument at dinner.
She has forborne every provocation for a month.
A good editor forbears where a proud one would argue.
The neighbors forbore for years before they complained.
We have forborne long enough.
Lenders may forbear for up to twelve months.
The servicer forbore while she was out of work.
The bank had forborne on the loan for two quarters.

senses.head: Refrain from doing something
body: Formal. Takes from + -ing, or, more literary still, a bare infinitive: he forbore to answer. (воздерживаться от, удерживаться)
examples: Please forbear from calling before nine.
He forbore to mention the argument at dinner.
She has forborne every provocation for a month.

senses.head: Be patient, show restraint
body: Without an object: to put up with something instead of reacting. The noun forbearance is more common than the verb. (проявлять терпение, сдерживаться)
examples: A good editor forbears where a proud one would argue.
The neighbors forbore for years before they complained.
We have forborne long enough.

senses.head: Hold off on collecting a debt
body: A banking term: a lender pauses payments instead of declaring default. You will meet it as the noun forbearance on loan paperwork. (предоставлять отсрочку (по кредиту))
examples: Lenders may forbear for up to twelve months.
The servicer forbore while she was out of work.
The bank had forborne on the loan for two quarters.

entries.register: rare — a formal prefixed verb; Americans say hold back or refrain
entries.contrast: A prefixed bear, so the vowels move the same way — but the participle keeps its e: forborne, never ✗ forborn. Do not confuse the verb forbear /fɔrˈbɛr/ "hold back" with the noun forebear /ˈfɔrˌbɛr/ "ancestor," which has an extra e and stresses the first syllable.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, though what it describes is deliberate inaction; formal and prefixed, where Americans say hold back or refrain
entries.transitivity: intransitive in practice — it takes from + -ing, a bare infinitive, or nothing at all (he forbore to answer, the neighbors forbore for years); the rare direct object (she has forborne every provocation) is literary
entries.passive: no — with a from-phrase or an infinitive there is nothing to promote, and even the rare direct object refuses it: ✗ every provocation was forborne, ✗ the loan was forborne on.

entries.meaning: To fail to remember something — a fact, an intention, an object left behind — or to deliberately put it out of your mind.
examples: I always forget where I parked.
She forgot his name halfway through the introduction.
She has forgotten more about engines than I ever knew.
Don't forget to lock the back door.
He forgot to set the alarm.
We had forgotten to book a table.
Try not to forget your badge again.
He forgot his passport at the hotel.
I have forgotten my umbrella in three cabs this year.
Forget about work for one weekend.
She never forgot what he said that night.
We had forgotten how loud the city gets in summer.
Forget it — it wasn't important.
'Can I borrow the truck?' 'Forget it.'
He forgot himself and raised his voice at the front desk.
She had never forgotten herself in public before.

senses.head: Fail to remember
body: The core sense. In American English the participle is forgotten without exception: ✗ I have forgot his name. (забывать, забыть)
examples: I always forget where I parked.
She forgot his name halfway through the introduction.
She has forgotten more about engines than I ever knew.

senses.head: Fail to do something you meant to
body: With an infinitive. Compare forget doing, which means failing to remember an event that already happened — a different thing entirely. (забыть сделать)
examples: Don't forget to lock the back door.
He forgot to set the alarm.
We had forgotten to book a table.

senses.head: Leave something behind
body: Ordinary in speech, though careful writers use leave once the place is named: I left my passport at the hotel. (забыть (вещь где-л.))
examples: Try not to forget your badge again.
He forgot his passport at the hotel.
I have forgotten my umbrella in three cabs this year.

senses.head: Put out of your mind, stop dwelling on
body: Deliberate rather than accidental, usually with about. This is the sense in forgive and forget. (забыть о, выбросить из головы)
examples: Forget about work for one weekend.
She never forgot what he said that night.
We had forgotten how loud the city gets in summer.

senses.head: forget it
body: A frozen imperative that means 'never mind', 'don't mention it', or a flat refusal, depending entirely on tone. (забудь; не стоит благодарности; ни за что)
examples: Forget it — it wasn't important.
'Can I borrow the truck?' 'Forget it.'

senses.head: forget yourself
body: Reflexive and somewhat dated: to behave improperly because you lost your composure. (забыться, потерять контроль над собой)
examples: He forgot himself and raised his voice at the front desk.
She had never forgotten herself in public before.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Forgotten is the American participle without exception: ✓ I have forgotten his name, ✗ I have forgot his name. British English tolerates bare forgot after have, and older texts use it freely, but in American writing it reads as an error. Note the American vowel too — forgot rhymes with hot /ɑ/, not with the rounded British /ɒ/.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the sense of an event that happens to you rather than one you perform; the progressive is limited but possible (I'm forgetting names lately). Forget it is a frozen imperative
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object may be a noun (forget your badge), a clause (I forget where I parked), or a to-infinitive (don't forget to lock the door); it is left out only in fixed uses
entries.passive: restricted — natural with a noun object (the whole affair had been forgotten by then, his name has been forgotten), impossible with an infinitive or clause complement: ✗ to set the alarm was forgotten by him.

entries.meaning: To give something up formally, or to renounce it under oath — the prefixed sibling of swear.
examples: The monks here forswear private property.
He forswore sugar in January and lasted nine days.
She has forsworn social media entirely.
I forswear nothing until I've slept on it.
After the audit they forswore cash payments altogether.
He had forsworn gambling twice before.
A man who forswears himself in court risks prison.
The witness had forsworn himself twice before the trial ended.

senses.head: Renounce, give up formally
body: Formal, and stronger than give up: it implies a public or binding commitment. (отрекаться от, отказываться от)
examples: The monks here forswear private property.
He forswore sugar in January and lasted nine days.
She has forsworn social media entirely.

senses.head: Swear never to do something again
body: With a noun or an -ing form. Close to swear off, which is the everyday American phrasing. (зарекаться)
examples: I forswear nothing until I've slept on it.
After the audit they forswore cash payments altogether.
He had forsworn gambling twice before.

senses.head: forswear yourself — perjure yourself
body: Reflexive and legal: to lie under oath. A forsworn witness is a perjurer, not someone who has renounced something. (лжесвидетельствовать, нарушить клятву)
examples: A man who forswears himself in court risks prison.
The witness had forsworn himself twice before the trial ended.

entries.register: rare — a formal prefixed verb, mostly legal or literary; renounce does the work
entries.contrast: A prefixed swear, with the same three vowels and the same ✗ have forswore trap. One extra wrinkle: used reflexively, forswear yourself means to lie under oath, so a forsworn witness is a perjurer, not someone who has given something up.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and performative: saying it is doing it. Formal and legal; forsworn also works as an adjective, and a forsworn witness is a perjurer, not a renouncer
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory — a noun, an -ing form, or a reflexive pronoun: they forswore cash payments, a man who forswears himself in court; ✗ he forswore on its own
entries.passive: restricted — possible in the renouncing sense but rare and formal (private property is forsworn here), and the reflexive perjury sense has none: ✗ himself was forsworn by the witness.

entries.meaning: To turn to ice or be gripped by cold — and figuratively to stop dead, to stop responding, or to hold money and prices where they are.
examples: Lakes up north freeze by early December.
The pond froze solid overnight.
The ground had frozen before they could dig.
You'll freeze out there without a hat.
We froze on the sidelines for two hours.
I have frozen at every one of his games this season.
Freeze the extra soup in small containers.
She froze six quarts of berries in August.
We have frozen half the batch already.
Deer freeze in headlights.
She froze when she heard footsteps behind her.
He had frozen halfway down the ladder.
The app freezes whenever I open a large file.
The video froze right at the punchline.
My laptop has frozen three times today.
The board voted to freeze tuition for a year.
The company froze hiring in March.
The state has frozen utility rates twice since 2020.
A judge can freeze an account within hours.
The bank froze the card after two odd charges.
Regulators have frozen the firm's assets.
They freeze out anyone who asks questions.
The partners froze him out of the decision.
Small vendors have been frozen out of the market.
Some people freeze up on camera.
He froze up during the interview.
I have frozen up in front of an audience more than once.

senses.head: Turn to ice, become frozen
body: The literal sense, intransitive. After have it is always frozen: ✗ the pipes have froze. (замерзать, застывать)
examples: Lakes up north freeze by early December.
The pond froze solid overnight.
The ground had frozen before they could dig.

senses.head: Be painfully cold (of a person)
body: Hyperbolic and usually progressive — I'm freezing — or in freeze to death, which almost never means literally dying. (мерзнуть, замерзать)
examples: You'll freeze out there without a hat.
We froze on the sidelines for two hours.
I have frozen at every one of his games this season.

senses.head: Preserve food by freezing
body: Transitive and everyday. The participle doubles as the familiar adjective: frozen peas, frozen dinner. (замораживать (продукты))
examples: Freeze the extra soup in small containers.
She froze six quarts of berries in August.
We have frozen half the batch already.

senses.head: Stop moving suddenly
body: Of a person or animal stopped by fear or surprise. The police command Freeze! comes from here. (застыть, замереть)
examples: Deer freeze in headlights.
She froze when she heard footsteps behind her.
He had frozen halfway down the ladder.

senses.head: Of a screen or program: stop responding
body: The standard computing use, intransitive, and the one learners meet daily. (зависать (о компьютере, программе))
examples: The app freezes whenever I open a large file.
The video froze right at the punchline.
My laptop has frozen three times today.

senses.head: Hold prices, wages, or hiring in place
body: Transitive, from business and government. The matching noun is a freeze: a hiring freeze. (заморозить (цены, зарплаты, найм))
examples: The board voted to freeze tuition for a year.
The company froze hiring in March.
The state has frozen utility rates twice since 2020.

senses.head: Block access to money or assets
body: A legal and banking use: a court, a bank, or a regulator makes funds untouchable. (заблокировать (счета, активы))
examples: A judge can freeze an account within hours.
The bank froze the card after two odd charges.
Regulators have frozen the firm's assets.

senses.head: freeze out — exclude
body: To shut someone out of a group, a deal, or a market by treating them as though they were not there. (вытеснять, отстранять, игнорировать)
examples: They freeze out anyone who asks questions.
The partners froze him out of the decision.
Small vendors have been frozen out of the market.

senses.head: freeze up — lock up, be unable to act
body: Of a person going blank under pressure, and of a mechanism seizing. (растеряться, оцепенеть; заклинить)
examples: Some people freeze up on camera.
He froze up during the interview.
I have frozen up in front of an audience more than once.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.third person: freezes · -ing form: freezing (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: ✗ The pipes have froze — after have, use frozen. Frozen also does heavy duty as an adjective (frozen peas, a frozen account), so the participle is the form learners already know by sight; the mistake is reaching for the bare past instead. The base is a homophone of frieze.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and ergative (the pond froze / she froze the berries); frozen does heavy duty as an adjective (frozen peas, a frozen account)
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive of ice, people, and software (the pond froze solid, my laptop has frozen), transitive of food, money, and rates (the board voted to freeze tuition)
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — regulators have frozen the firm's assets → the firm's assets have been frozen, small vendors have been frozen out of the market. No passive of the intransitive the ground had frozen.
entries.phrasal verbs: freeze out · freeze over · freeze up

entries.meaning: To put something where it cannot be found, to go where you cannot be seen, or to keep something secret.
examples: We hide the gifts in the attic every year.
He hid the spare key under a flowerpot.
Someone has hidden the remote again.
Kids hide behind the couch during thunderstorms.
She hid in the stairwell until they left.
The cat had hidden under the porch all afternoon.
She doesn't hide her opinions.
The report hid the real numbers in a footnote.
He has hidden the diagnosis from his family for months.
Clouds hide the summit most mornings.
A hedge hid the house from the road.
The path had been hidden by new snow.
Suspects usually hide out with relatives.
He hid out in a motel for a week.
They have hidden out in the mountains since the indictment.

senses.head: Put something out of sight
body: Transitive and literal. The participle is hidden: ✗ he has hid the key. (прятать, спрятать)
examples: We hide the gifts in the attic every year.
He hid the spare key under a flowerpot.
Someone has hidden the remote again.

senses.head: Conceal yourself
body: Intransitive, of people and animals getting out of view. (прятаться, скрываться)
examples: Kids hide behind the couch during thunderstorms.
She hid in the stairwell until they left.
The cat had hidden under the porch all afternoon.

senses.head: Keep secret, conceal facts or feelings
body: Figurative and very common: information, a diagnosis, an emotion, a number in a footnote. (скрывать, утаивать)
examples: She doesn't hide her opinions.
The report hid the real numbers in a footnote.
He has hidden the diagnosis from his family for months.

senses.head: Cover from view
body: Of a thing that blocks sight of something else — clouds, a hedge, snow — with no intention involved. (заслонять, закрывать (собой))
examples: Clouds hide the summit most mornings.
A hedge hid the house from the road.
The path had been hidden by new snow.

senses.head: hide out, go into hiding
body: To stay concealed somewhere for a stretch of time, usually from the police, the press, or an obligation. (скрываться, отсиживаться)
examples: Suspects usually hide out with relatives.
He hid out in a motel for a week.
They have hidden out in the mountains since the indictment.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.third person: hides · -ing form: hiding (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: The past is hid and the participle is hidden: ✗ He has hid the key, ✓ He has hidden the key. Hidden is common as an adjective too (a hidden cost, hidden fees), which makes it easy to recall. Note that hide is also a noun meaning an animal's skin.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, whether deliberate (he hid the key) or not (clouds hide the summit); hidden is also a common adjective, as in hidden fees
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a thing or fact concealed (the report hid the real numbers), intransitive when you conceal yourself (she hid in the stairwell, they hid out for a week)
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the path had been hidden by new snow, the remote has been hidden again. No passive of the intransitive the cat hid under the porch.
entries.phrasal verbs: hide away · hide behind · hide from · hide out

entries.meaning: To weave two or more things together — threads literally, stories, lives, or themes figuratively.
examples: Weavers here interweave wool and linen in the same cloth.
The artist interwove copper wire and silk thread.
Craftsmen have interwoven the two fibers for centuries.
Good novels interweave several lives without losing any of them.
The score interweaves three folk melodies.
Their families had interwoven through four generations of marriages.
The two plots have interwoven so tightly you cannot follow one alone.
Politics and money are thoroughly interwoven here.
The two economies are deeply interwoven.

senses.head: Weave strands together
body: The literal textile sense, transitive. Unlike plain weave, it has no regular alternative: ✗ interweaved. (переплетать, вплетать (нити))
examples: Weavers here interweave wool and linen in the same cloth.
The artist interwove copper wire and silk thread.
Craftsmen have interwoven the two fibers for centuries.

senses.head: Work several elements into a whole
body: Where the verb actually lives in modern writing — of plots, melodies, arguments, and families. (сплетать, переплетать (сюжеты, темы))
examples: Good novels interweave several lives without losing any of them.
The score interweaves three folk melodies.
Their families had interwoven through four generations of marriages.
The two plots have interwoven so tightly you cannot follow one alone.

senses.head: interwoven — closely connected (adjective)
body: The participle does most of this verb's work in real American prose: interwoven storylines, interwoven fates. (тесно связанный, переплетенный)
examples: Politics and money are thoroughly interwoven here.
The two economies are deeply interwoven.

entries.register: rare — a prefixed derivative; only the participle interwoven sees much use
entries.third person: interweaves · -ing form: interweaving (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: A prefixed weave with identical forms. In real American writing the participle interwoven does nearly all the work — interwoven storylines, interwoven fates — and the finite past interwove is rare. Unlike plain weave, it does not have a regular alternative: ✗ interweaved.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; in real American prose the participle interwoven does most of the work, as an adjective (interwoven storylines) or a predicate (the two economies are deeply interwoven)
entries.transitivity: both — normally transitive (the artist interwove copper wire and silk thread, good novels interweave several lives), occasionally intransitive of the strands themselves (the two plots have interwoven so tightly you cannot follow one alone)
entries.passive: yes — the two fibers have been interwoven for centuries, three folk melodies are interwoven in the score; the passive and the adjectival participle are where this verb actually lives.

entries.meaning: To say the wrong thing by mistake — in American public life, the standard way to take a statement back without calling it a lie.
examples: If I misspeak, please correct me.
The senator misspoke about the date of the vote.
He admits he has misspoken twice this week.
Even careful people misspeak when they are tired.
The announcer misspoke the winner's name on live television.
She realized she had misspoken the moment the words left her mouth.

senses.head: Misstate something, say the wrong thing
body: Nearly always about oneself and nearly always in the past: I misspoke concedes an error while denying intent. (оговориться, сказать не то)
examples: If I misspeak, please correct me.
The senator misspoke about the date of the vote.
He admits he has misspoken twice this week.

senses.head: Say or pronounce badly
body: The older, plainer sense — getting a word, a name, or a line out wrong. Rarer than the political use above. (говорить или произносить неправильно)
examples: Even careful people misspeak when they are tired.
The announcer misspoke the winner's name on live television.
She realized she had misspoken the moment the words left her mouth.

entries.register: neutral — current American usage, but almost always as I misspoke
entries.contrast: A prefixed speak: same forms, plus a spelling trap — two s's, because mis- runs straight into speak. In American public life I misspoke is the standard way to walk back a statement without calling it a lie, so you will meet the past far more often than any other form.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and in American public life nearly frozen in the first-person past: I misspoke concedes an error while denying intent
entries.transitivity: both — usually intransitive (if I misspeak, please correct me), transitive in the older plain sense of getting a word out wrong (the announcer misspoke the winner's name)
entries.passive: restricted — marginal even with an object (?the winner's name was misspoken on live television), and the ordinary intransitive use has no passive at all: ✗ it was misspoken by the senator.

entries.meaning: To use the voice to say words — to talk, to hold a conversation, to use a language, or to address an audience.
examples: Please speak more slowly.
He spoke very quietly.
Nobody had spoken for a full minute.
Speak with your advisor before you drop the class.
I spoke to the landlord yesterday.
She has spoken with all three references.
We speak Spanish at home.
She spoke almost no English when she arrived.
I have spoken Russian since childhood.
The dean speaks at every graduation.
He spoke for twenty minutes without notes.
She has spoken at three conferences this year.
Speak up, please — we can't hear you in back.
Nobody spoke up when he asked for volunteers.
One student has spoken up at every meeting.
Few employees speak out in meetings like that.
Teachers spoke out against the new schedule.
Several officers have spoken out since the report.
She speaks her mind at every meeting.
He spoke his mind and lost the account.
I have spoken my mind often enough here.
I speak for the whole department here.
She spoke for the family at the hearing.
He has spoken for that community for twenty years.
The numbers speak for themselves.
Her silence spoke volumes.
The results have spoken for themselves all season.
He's the mayor of this block, so to speak.
Speaking of rent, mine went up again.

senses.head: Say words, talk
body: The bare sense, usually with an adverb or in the negative. This is the model verb for the whole group: ✗ I have spoke. (говорить, разговаривать)
examples: Please speak more slowly.
He spoke very quietly.
Nobody had spoken for a full minute.

senses.head: speak to, speak with — talk to someone
body: Speak to and speak with are both American; with sounds a shade more mutual, to a shade more one-directional. (поговорить с, обратиться к)
examples: Speak with your advisor before you drop the class.
I spoke to the landlord yesterday.
She has spoken with all three references.

senses.head: Know and use a language
body: Transitive, with a language as the object, and never progressive in this sense: ✗ I am speaking Spanish to mean you know it. (говорить на (языке), владеть языком)
examples: We speak Spanish at home.
She spoke almost no English when she arrived.
I have spoken Russian since childhood.

senses.head: Give a talk, address an audience
body: Intransitive, usually with at, to, or on. The related noun is speaker. (выступать, произносить речь)
examples: The dean speaks at every graduation.
He spoke for twenty minutes without notes.
She has spoken at three conferences this year.

senses.head: speak up
body: Two everyday uses: talk louder so you can be heard, and volunteer an opinion or an offer in a group. (говорить громче; подать голос)
examples: Speak up, please — we can't hear you in back.
Nobody spoke up when he asked for volunteers.
One student has spoken up at every meeting.

senses.head: speak out
body: Stronger than speak up: to state a public objection, usually at some risk. Often speak out against. (открыто высказываться, выступать против)
examples: Few employees speak out in meetings like that.
Teachers spoke out against the new schedule.
Several officers have spoken out since the report.

senses.head: speak your mind
body: A fixed phrase for saying exactly what you think, with the implication that most people would not. (высказать свое мнение прямо)
examples: She speaks her mind at every meeting.
He spoke his mind and lost the account.
I have spoken my mind often enough here.

senses.head: speak for — represent; vouch for
body: To act as someone's voice, or to attest to their quality. Speak for yourself is a mild rebuke. (говорить от имени; ручаться за)
examples: I speak for the whole department here.
She spoke for the family at the hearing.
He has spoken for that community for twenty years.

senses.head: speak for itself, speak volumes
body: Fixed phrases with a thing as the subject: the evidence needs no comment. (говорить само за себя, быть красноречивым)
examples: The numbers speak for themselves.
Her silence spoke volumes.
The results have spoken for themselves all season.

senses.head: so to speak, generally speaking
body: Frozen phrases used as sentence adverbs — hedging a metaphor, framing a generalization, or changing the subject with speaking of. (так сказать; вообще говоря)
examples: He's the mayor of this block, so to speak.
Speaking of rent, mine went up again.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: ✗ I have spoke to her — the participle is spoken. This is the model verb for the whole group, so fixing it here fixes bespeak, misspeak, and by analogy break, steal, and freeze. Note that spoke is also a noun (a wheel's spoke) and spoken runs loose as an adjective in spoken English, soft-spoken, well-spoken.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the talking senses (he spoke for twenty minutes), but stative when it means knowing a language, where the progressive is out: ✗ I am speaking Spanish to mean you know it
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive at the core (please speak more slowly, nobody had spoken for a minute), transitive with a language or a fixed object (we speak Spanish at home, she speaks her mind)
entries.passive: restricted — natural with a language or a fixed object (Spanish is spoken here, not a word was spoken), but the ordinary intransitive and prepositional uses have none: ✗ the landlord was spoken, and ✗ she was spoken to slowly only works as the separate prepositional passive.
entries.phrasal verbs: speak for · speak out · speak to · speak up · speak up for

entries.meaning: To take what is not yours — and by extension to move quietly, to snatch a small pleasure, or to take the attention away from someone else.
examples: Raccoons steal food right off the grill.
Someone stole my umbrella from the lobby.
Two paintings have been stolen from the museum.
He learned his car had been stolen only that morning.
Big labels steal from small ones all the time.
He stole the line from an old movie.
She claims they have stolen her design.
I steal twenty minutes with a book after lunch.
He stole a look at his phone under the table.
We have stolen whole afternoons this way.
Fog steals up the valley every evening.
She stole out of the house before dawn.
He had stolen back to his seat unnoticed.
She steals every scene she is in.
The dog stole the show at the wedding.
That trumpet solo has stolen the whole record.
Don't let the opening act steal your thunder.
He stole her thunder by announcing it first.
The leak had stolen the mayor's thunder completely.
Fast runners steal bases in close games.
He stole second on the first pitch.
She has stolen thirty bases this season.

senses.head: Take without permission
body: The core sense. You steal the thing and rob the person or place: ✗ they stole the bank. The passive is where the participle error shows up: ✗ my bike has been stole. (красть, воровать)
examples: Raccoons steal food right off the grill.
Someone stole my umbrella from the lobby.
Two paintings have been stolen from the museum.
He learned his car had been stolen only that morning.

senses.head: Take an idea or work as your own
body: Of plagiarism, borrowed jokes, and copied designs — no physical object changes hands. (присваивать, воровать (идеи, чужую работу))
examples: Big labels steal from small ones all the time.
He stole the line from an old movie.
She claims they have stolen her design.

senses.head: Take quickly and quietly
body: Of a glance, a kiss, a nap, an hour — something small taken when nobody is looking or when there is no time for it. (урвать, сделать украдкой)
examples: I steal twenty minutes with a book after lunch.
He stole a look at his phone under the table.
We have stolen whole afternoons this way.

senses.head: Move quietly, sneak
body: Intransitive and literary, usually with a direction: steal away, steal into, steal out. (красться, пробираться)
examples: Fog steals up the valley every evening.
She stole out of the house before dawn.
He had stolen back to his seat unnoticed.

senses.head: steal the show, steal the scene
body: To attract all the attention at an event, usually without meaning to and usually from a smaller role. (затмить всех, украсть все внимание)
examples: She steals every scene she is in.
The dog stole the show at the wedding.
That trumpet solo has stolen the whole record.

senses.head: steal someone's thunder
body: To take the credit or the moment someone else had prepared, typically by getting there first. (перехватить инициативу, присвоить чужие лавры)
examples: Don't let the opening act steal your thunder.
He stole her thunder by announcing it first.
The leak had stolen the mayor's thunder completely.

senses.head: steal a base (baseball)
body: To advance a base while the pitch is being thrown, without a hit. A standard American sports use with its own statistic, stolen bases. (украсть базу (в бейсболе))
examples: Fast runners steal bases in close games.
He stole second on the first pitch.
She has stolen thirty bases this season.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: ✗ My bike has been stole — the participle is stolen, and the passive is where the error shows up most, because this verb is so often reported rather than performed. Steal is a homophone of steel, and the past stole is also a noun for a long shawl or a priest's vestment.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the taking senses and the quiet-movement sense (she stole out of the house) share one form but behave differently
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the thing taken (someone stole my umbrella; you steal the thing but rob the person: ✗ they stole the bank), intransitive with from or a direction (big labels steal from small ones, fog steals up the valley)
entries.passive: yes in the taking senses, and this is where the participle error shows: two paintings have been stolen from the museum, ✗ my bike has been stole. No passive of the movement sense: ✗ out of the house was stolen.

entries.meaning: To make a solemn promise or take an oath — and, in the everyday sense, to use profanity.
examples: My uncle swears every time his team loses.
He swore at the referee and got thrown out.
She has never sworn in front of the kids.
Witnesses swear to tell the truth.
They swore an oath of loyalty.
He has sworn to finish what she started.
I swear I locked the door.
She swore she had mailed the check.
He has sworn up and down that he never saw the email.
They swear in the new council on Monday.
The chief justice swore him in on the Capitol steps.
The jury had been sworn in before lunch.
People swear off sugar every January.
She swore off cable and never looked back.
He has sworn off coffee after six o'clock.
My mother swears by this cough syrup.
He swore by that mechanic for thirty years.
Runners have sworn by these shoes for a decade.

senses.head: Use profanity
body: Intransitive, with at someone or about something. The commonest sense in speech; curse is the more formal synonym. (ругаться, материться)
examples: My uncle swears every time his team loses.
He swore at the referee and got thrown out.
She has never sworn in front of the kids.

senses.head: Make a solemn promise or oath
body: The formal sense, with to + verb or with a noun object: swear an oath, swear allegiance. The participle is sworn: ✗ I have swore. (клясться, присягать)
examples: Witnesses swear to tell the truth.
They swore an oath of loyalty.
He has sworn to finish what she started.

senses.head: Insist emphatically
body: I swear plus a clause — a way of pressing a claim when you expect not to be believed. Informal. (божиться, уверять)
examples: I swear I locked the door.
She swore she had mailed the check.
He has sworn up and down that he never saw the email.

senses.head: swear someone in
body: Of officials, juries, and witnesses taking office or the stand. Usually passive: the jury was sworn in. (приводить к присяге)
examples: They swear in the new council on Monday.
The chief justice swore him in on the Capitol steps.
The jury had been sworn in before lunch.

senses.head: swear off
body: To give up a habit deliberately and announce it — coffee, cable, late nights. (зарекаться, отказываться от (привычки))
examples: People swear off sugar every January.
She swore off cable and never looked back.
He has sworn off coffee after six o'clock.

senses.head: swear by
body: To have complete faith in a remedy, a brand, or a method. Not to be confused with swear at, which is the profanity sense. (полностью доверять, души не чаять в)
examples: My mother swears by this cough syrup.
He swore by that mechanic for thirty years.
Runners have sworn by these shoes for a decade.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: ✗ I have swore — the participle drops the e: sworn. Two unrelated senses share the verb, making an oath (sworn in as mayor) and using profanity (he swore at the referee), and only context tells you which one you are reading.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both unrelated senses, taking an oath and using profanity; sworn also serves as an adjective (a sworn statement, sworn testimony)
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in the profanity sense and with at / by / off (he swore at the referee, my mother swears by this cough syrup), transitive with an oath, a clause, or a person (they swore an oath, I swear I locked the door, they swear in the new council Monday)
entries.passive: yes in the oath senses, and usually preferred there — the jury had been sworn in before lunch, witnesses are sworn before testifying. The profanity sense allows only the prepositional passive (the referee was sworn at), and swear by refuses it: ✗ that mechanic was sworn by.
entries.phrasal verbs: swear at · swear by · swear in · swear off · swear to

entries.meaning: To pull something apart by force — and, of a person or vehicle, to move very fast. The verb tear /tɛr/ rhymes with air; the noun tear /tɪr/ that means a drop from the eye is a different word.
examples: Please don't tear the wrapping paper.
He tore the letter into four pieces.
The storm had torn the awning loose.
Thin paper tears if you pull it flat.
The seam tore the first time he wore it.
My jacket has torn at the elbow.
Storms like that tear shingles right off the roof.
She tore the page out of the notebook.
He has torn himself away from that screen exactly once today.
Runners tear muscles when they skip the warm-up.
He tore a ligament in the second half.
She has torn the same hamstring twice.
The town was torn between two proposals.
I am torn between the two offers.
She had been torn about it for weeks.
Kids tear around the yard until dark.
He tore out of the driveway without looking.
The truck had torn past us on the shoulder.
Developers tear down houses like that every week.
She tore up the contract in front of him.
The scandal has torn the party apart.

senses.head: Rip, pull apart
body: The core transitive sense. After have it is torn: ✗ I have tore it. (рвать, разрывать)
examples: Please don't tear the wrapping paper.
He tore the letter into four pieces.
The storm had torn the awning loose.

senses.head: Come apart, get ripped
body: The intransitive half of the same idea, with the fabric or paper as the subject. (рваться, порваться)
examples: Thin paper tears if you pull it flat.
The seam tore the first time he wore it.
My jacket has torn at the elbow.

senses.head: Wrench away, pull off by force
body: With from, out of, or off. Also reflexive — tear yourself away from something absorbing. (вырывать, отрывать)
examples: Storms like that tear shingles right off the roof.
She tore the page out of the notebook.
He has torn himself away from that screen exactly once today.

senses.head: Injure a muscle or ligament
body: Standard sports-medicine use; the matching noun is a tear /tɛr/ — an ACL tear. (порвать (мышцу, связку))
examples: Runners tear muscles when they skip the warm-up.
He tore a ligament in the second half.
She has torn the same hamstring twice.

senses.head: be torn between — passive
body: Passive only, of a person or a group pulled two ways by loyalties or options. (разрываться между)
examples: The town was torn between two proposals.
I am torn between the two offers.
She had been torn about it for weeks.

senses.head: Move very fast
body: Informal and intransitive, always with a direction: tear down the street, tear out of the lot, tear around. (мчаться, нестись)
examples: Kids tear around the yard until dark.
He tore out of the driveway without looking.
The truck had torn past us on the shoulder.

senses.head: tear down, tear up, tear apart
body: Tear down is to demolish a building or discredit a person; tear up is to rip to shreds (and, from the noun, to start crying, /tɪr/); tear apart is to destroy or divide. (сносить; разорвать в клочья; разнести, расколоть)
examples: Developers tear down houses like that every week.
She tore up the contract in front of him.
The scandal has torn the party apart.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: A true homograph: the verb tear "rip" is /tɛr/ and rhymes with air, while the noun tear "drop from the eye" is /tɪr/ and rhymes with ear. Same spelling, two different words — the noun's plural tears is /tɪrz/, the verb's third person tears is /tɛrz/. And ✗ I have tore it: after have it is torn.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and ergative (he tore the letter / the seam tore); the fast-movement sense (he tore out of the driveway) is a separate informal use, and tear /tɛr/ is a different word from the noun tear /tɪr/
entries.transitivity: both — transitive when you rip or wrench something (she tore the page out of the notebook, he tore a ligament), intransitive when the fabric gives way or someone moves fast (my jacket has torn at the elbow, kids tear around the yard)
entries.passive: yes in the ripping senses — the awning had been torn loose by the storm. Be torn between is passive-only, with no active counterpart: I am torn between the two offers, ✗ the two offers tear me between. No passive of the movement sense.
entries.phrasal verbs: tear apart · tear at · tear away · tear down · tear into · tear off · tear out · tear through · tear up

entries.meaning: To release something from a frozen state — ice, money, prices, or a stuck screen.
examples: Run warm water over the joint to unfreeze the pipe.
Warm rain unfroze the top layer of soil.
The line has unfrozen on its own.
Sanctions relief would unfreeze billions.
The court unfroze the family's bank accounts in April.
Congress has unfrozen the aid package.
The board voted to unfreeze salaries in July.
The agency unfroze rates after the lawsuit.
The hiring budget had been unfrozen weeks before anyone noticed.
A restart usually unfreezes the screen.
Nothing unfroze the app but a full reboot.
The update has unfrozen the interface for most users.

senses.head: Thaw, release from ice
body: The literal sense. For food Americans normally say thaw or defrost; unfreeze survives mainly for pipes, locks, and ground. (размораживать, оттаивать)
examples: Run warm water over the joint to unfreeze the pipe.
Warm rain unfroze the top layer of soil.
The line has unfrozen on its own.

senses.head: Release blocked funds or assets
body: The commonest use in the news, usually of a court, a bank, or a government reversing a freeze. (разблокировать (счета, средства))
examples: Sanctions relief would unfreeze billions.
The court unfroze the family's bank accounts in April.
Congress has unfrozen the aid package.

senses.head: Lift a freeze on prices, wages, or hiring
body: The administrative counterpart of freeze: budgets, salaries, tuition, and rents go back to moving. (отменить заморозку (цен, найма))
examples: The board voted to unfreeze salaries in July.
The agency unfroze rates after the lawsuit.
The hiring budget had been unfrozen weeks before anyone noticed.

senses.head: Get a stuck screen or program going again
body: Everyday computing use, transitive. Note that the finite past unfroze sounds odd to many readers here; got it unfrozen is commoner in speech. (разморозить, оживить (экран, программу))
examples: A restart usually unfreezes the screen.
Nothing unfroze the app but a full reboot.
The update has unfrozen the interface for most users.

entries.register: rare — a prefixed derivative; for food Americans say thaw or defrost, and unfroze reads oddly
entries.third person: unfreezes · -ing form: unfreezing (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: A prefixed freeze, inflecting the same way — but in practice Americans use the base and the participle far more than the past: unfreeze the account, the funds are still unfrozen. For food, thaw and defrost have taken the job over, and the finite past unfroze is rare enough that many readers find it odd on the page.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and ergative like its base freeze (the court unfroze the accounts / the line has unfrozen); in practice the base and the participle carry the verb, and the finite past unfroze reads oddly to many Americans
entries.transitivity: both — transitive of funds, rates, and screens (sanctions relief would unfreeze billions, a restart usually unfreezes the screen), intransitive of the thing thawing on its own (the line has unfrozen)
entries.passive: yes — the hiring budget had been unfrozen weeks before anyone noticed, the family's accounts were unfrozen in April; the participle also stands as an adjective (the funds are still unfrozen).

entries.meaning: To stop sleeping, or to rouse someone from sleep — in everyday American speech almost always with up.
examples: I wake at six without an alarm.
She woke twice in the night.
He has woken at odd hours ever since the trip.
Try not to wake anyone on your way out.
The thunder woke the baby.
The dog had woken us before the alarm went off.
Wake up — we're here.
He woke up on the couch again.
She has woken up early all week.
We wake up to these things too late.
The industry finally woke up to the problem.
Voters have woken up to what it costs.
Old letters wake feelings you thought were done with.
The song woke something in her.
The election had woken a part of the state nobody had polled.

senses.head: Stop sleeping
body: Intransitive. American edited prose wants woken after have; British English tolerates have woke, and the regular waked is also allowed but sounds dated. (просыпаться)
examples: I wake at six without an alarm.
She woke twice in the night.
He has woken at odd hours ever since the trip.

senses.head: Rouse someone from sleep
body: Transitive. Keep it clear of the slang adjective woke, which is unrelated to the verb's tenses. (будить, разбудить)
examples: Try not to wake anyone on your way out.
The thunder woke the baby.
The dog had woken us before the alarm went off.

senses.head: wake up
body: The ordinary spoken form, both intransitive and transitive. As an imperative it also means 'pay attention, face facts'. (просыпаться, вставать; очнуться)
examples: Wake up — we're here.
He woke up on the couch again.
She has woken up early all week.

senses.head: wake up to — become aware of
body: To finally register a problem that has been there all along. (осознать, спохватиться)
examples: We wake up to these things too late.
The industry finally woke up to the problem.
Voters have woken up to what it costs.

senses.head: Stir up, rouse (feelings, memories)
body: Figurative and transitive; the more literary awake covers the same ground. (пробуждать, будить (чувства))
examples: Old letters wake feelings you thought were done with.
The song woke something in her.
The election had woken a part of the state nobody had polled.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.third person: wakes · -ing form: waking (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: American English also allows the regular waked, but woke/woken is the ordinary choice and wake up beats bare wake in speech. British English often uses woke as the participle (have woke); American edited prose wants woken. Keep the verb separate from the slang adjective woke, and from the related verbs awake and the regular awaken/awakened.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and ergative between sleeping and rousing (she woke twice / the thunder woke the baby). Nothing to do with the slang adjective woke
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive when you stop sleeping (I wake at six without an alarm), transitive when you rouse a person or a feeling (the song woke something in her); wake up works both ways
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the baby was woken by the thunder, we had been woken before the alarm went off. No passive of the intransitive she woke twice in the night.

entries.meaning: To have clothing or an accessory on your body — and, in a second family of senses, to reduce or damage something gradually through use.
examples: Most people here wear boots all winter.
He wore the same tie to every interview.
She has worn those earrings every day this month.
She wears her hair short now.
He wore a look of complete confusion.
He has worn a beard since college.
Traffic wears the paint off the crosswalk every year.
Water wore a channel through the rock.
The stairs had worn smooth in the middle.
Cheap fabric wears badly.
The soles wore out in a single season.
The rug has worn through by the door.
Those kids wear me out.
He wore out three pairs of shoes on the trail.
