I have worn myself out arguing about this.
Wait until the numbness wears off.
The novelty wore off in a week.
The excitement has worn off completely.
Constant delays wear down even patient clients.
They wore him down with phone calls.
The campaign had worn her down by October.
His whistling wears on me.
As the afternoon wore on, fewer people stayed.
The wait has worn on everyone.
He came in with a worn jacket and a worn face.
The book is worn at the spine.

senses.head: Have clothing on
body: The core sense, and one of the highest-frequency verbs in the language. After have it is worn: ✗ she has wore that coat. (носить (одежду), быть одетым в)
examples: Most people here wear boots all winter.
He wore the same tie to every interview.
She has worn those earrings every day this month.

senses.head: Have a hairstyle, expression, or look
body: Extends past clothes to anything you carry on your person or your face: a beard, a smile, a look of confusion, cologne. (носить (прическу); иметь (выражение лица))
examples: She wears her hair short now.
He wore a look of complete confusion.
He has worn a beard since college.

senses.head: Damage or reduce through use
body: Transitive, of friction over time: wear a hole, wear a groove, wear something smooth. (изнашивать, стирать, протирать)
examples: Traffic wears the paint off the crosswalk every year.
Water wore a channel through the rock.
The stairs had worn smooth in the middle.

senses.head: Become thin or damaged with use
body: The intransitive half. Wear well is a compliment — it means something (or someone) ages without deteriorating. (изнашиваться, протираться)
examples: Cheap fabric wears badly.
The soles wore out in a single season.
The rug has worn through by the door.

senses.head: wear out
body: Of an object used until it is useless, and of a person exhausted by something. Also wear out your welcome. (изнашивать(ся); измотать)
examples: Those kids wear me out.
He wore out three pairs of shoes on the trail.
I have worn myself out arguing about this.

senses.head: wear off
body: Of an effect fading: medication, novelty, shock, the numbness after the dentist. (проходить, ослабевать (об эффекте))
examples: Wait until the numbness wears off.
The novelty wore off in a week.
The excitement has worn off completely.

senses.head: wear down
body: To weaken someone's resistance by persistence rather than force; also literal, of surfaces ground away. (измотать, сломить сопротивление)
examples: Constant delays wear down even patient clients.
They wore him down with phone calls.
The campaign had worn her down by October.

senses.head: wear on
body: Two uses: of time passing slowly — as the evening wore on — and of something grating on a person. (тянуться (о времени); действовать на нервы)
examples: His whistling wears on me.
As the afternoon wore on, fewer people stayed.
The wait has worn on everyone.

senses.head: worn — shabby, tired (adjective)
body: The participle stands alone as an adjective, of objects and of faces — a useful reminder that worn, not wore, is the form that follows have and be. (потертый, изношенный; измученный)
examples: He came in with a worn jacket and a worn face.
The book is worn at the spine.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: ✗ She has wore that coat all winter — the participle is worn. Worn also stands alone as an adjective meaning shabby or tired (worn shoes, a worn face), which is a useful reminder that it, not wore, is the form that follows have and be. The base is a homophone of where and ware.
entries.verb type: both — the erosion senses are action and dynamic (water wore a channel through the rock), while having clothes on is closer to stative, a state that happens to allow the progressive for temporary wear (she's wearing boots today). Worn is also an adjective meaning shabby or tired
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with clothing, a look, or a surface (he wore the same tie, traffic wears the paint off), intransitive when the thing itself deteriorates or an effect fades (cheap fabric wears badly, the numbness wears off)
entries.passive: restricted — free in the erosion senses (the stairs had been worn smooth, he was worn down by the campaign), but the clothing sense is stilted as a full passive (✗ the same tie was worn by him to every interview) and survives mainly as a reduced participle: the coat worn by the bride.
entries.phrasal verbs: wear away · wear down · wear in · wear off · wear on · wear out

entries.meaning: To make cloth or baskets by crossing strands — and, figuratively, to work several elements into one whole. Winding through traffic is the regular weaved.
examples: They weave rugs on a loom older than the house.
Her grandmother wove blankets for the whole family.
Villagers here have woven silk for six generations.
The scarf is woven from two kinds of wool.
Children weave wreaths out of clover.
She wove a basket out of river reeds.
He had woven a fence out of willow branches.
He weaves jokes into serious lectures.
The author had woven the letters into the narrative.
She has woven three timelines into one story.
Cyclists weave through stopped traffic all day.
The runner weaved through the pack on the last lap.
He has weaved in and out of that lane for a mile.

senses.head: Make cloth on a loom
body: The literal textile sense, and the one that firmly takes wove/woven. (ткать)
examples: They weave rugs on a loom older than the house.
Her grandmother wove blankets for the whole family.
Villagers here have woven silk for six generations.
The scarf is woven from two kinds of wool.

senses.head: Make by interlacing strands
body: Baskets, wreaths, fences, hair — anything built by crossing flexible material. (плести (корзину, венок))
examples: Children weave wreaths out of clover.
She wove a basket out of river reeds.
He had woven a fence out of willow branches.

senses.head: Work several elements into a whole
body: Figurative, of stories, arguments, music, and lectures. Usually weave something into something. (вплетать, сплетать (в повествование))
examples: He weaves jokes into serious lectures.
The author had woven the letters into the narrative.
She has woven three timelines into one story.

senses.head: Move winding through
body: This sense is regular — weaved, weaved: ✓ the cab weaved across three lanes, ✗ the cab wove across three lanes. (лавировать, петлять)
examples: Cyclists weave through stopped traffic all day.
The runner weaved through the pack on the last lap.
He has weaved in and out of that lane for a mile.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary in speech and writing, above all the participle woven
entries.third person: weaves · -ing form: weaving (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: The meaning picks the forms. Weaving thread, baskets, or storylines takes wove/woven; moving in and out through traffic or a crowd takes the regular weaved: ✓ The cab weaved across three lanes, ✗ The cab wove across three lanes.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and the sense picks the forms: making cloth or storylines takes wove/woven, while winding through traffic is regular — ✓ the cab weaved across three lanes, ✗ the cab wove across three lanes
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the making senses (her grandmother wove blankets, he weaves jokes into serious lectures), intransitive in the movement sense (cyclists weave through stopped traffic)
entries.passive: yes in the making senses — the scarf is woven from two kinds of wool, the letters had been woven into the narrative. No passive of the movement sense: ✗ through the pack was weaved.
